'''''Meeting at Night''''' is an English love poem written by the [[Victorian literature|Victorian]] poet [[Robert Browning]]. Browning wrote the poem in two parts as "Night" and "Morning", (later separated as "Meeting at Night" and "[[Parting at Morning]]" in 1849) for his 1845 work ''[[Dramatic Romances and Lyrics]]''.

The poem (like others of the 1845 collection) was written during the courtship period of Browning with his future wife [[Elizabeth Barrett Browning|Elizabeth Barrett]]. Kennedy and Hair describes the poem as the most sensual poem of Browning.<ref name="KennedyHair2007">{{cite book|author1=Richard S. Kennedy|author2=Donald S. Hair|title=The Dramatic Imagination of Robert Browning: A Literary Life|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=_-4M5DIKJToC&pg=PA134|year=2007|publisher=University of Missouri Press|isbn=978-0-8262-6552-4|pages=134–136}}</ref>

== Background ==
[[John Kenyon]] a distant cousin of [[Elizabeth Barrett Browning|Elizabeth Barrett]] presented a copy of Barrett's [[Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Poems (1844)|1844 poems]] to Sarianna Browning, sister of Robert Browning. Browning discovering his name in print in the poem volume wrote a letter to Elizabeth on January 10, 1815. Upon getting the reply he sent the manuscripts of poems and plays of the [[Dramatic Romances and Lyrics]] for proofreading to her.<ref name="Pollock2003">{{cite book|author=Mary Sanders Pollock|title=Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning: A Creative Partnership|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=IfuY5sdwphYC&pg=PA61|date=1 January 2003|publisher=Ashgate Publishing, Ltd.|isbn=978-0-7546-3328-0|pages=61–62}}</ref>

The poems in [[Dramatic Romances and Lyrics]] were arranged in groups of two or three with the two love poems "Night" and "Morning" as complementary. Richard S. Kennedy, Donald S. Hair describes "... they present a compact dramatic narrative reflecting a decidedly masculine attitude toward love."<ref name="KennedyHair2007"></ref>

== Poem ==
'''''Meeting at Night''''' (excerpt)
<poem>
The grey sea and the long black land;
And the yellow half-moon large and low;
And the startled little waves that leap
In fiery ringlets from their sleep,
As I gain the cove with pushing prow,
And quench its speed i' the slushy sand.

Then a mile of warm sea-scented beach;
Three fields to cross till a farm appears;
A tap at the pane, the quick sharp scratch
And blue spurt of a lighted match,
And a voice less loud, thro' its joys and fears,
Than the two hearts beating each to each!
</poem>
* Read '''[[:wikisource:Meeting at Night|the full poem]]''' at [[Wikisource]]

== Themes ==
The poem is written in two stanzas of six lines each. The first stanza describes the excitement of the secret journey by a boat on the sea. The second stanza describes the fulfillment of the meeting of the two lovers.

Unlike its sister poem "Parting at Morning" which uses ''pronominal reference'' to attribute the gender of the person in the boat (as male) the poem never reveals the identity of the two lovers.<ref name="Conference2008">{{cite book|author=Poetics and Linguistics Association. Conference|title=The State of Stylistics: PALA 26|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=EpsEZl5FY1kC&pg=PA19|year=2008|publisher=Rodopi|isbn=978-90-420-2428-1|pages=19–21}}</ref> The poem follows the rhyme scheme ''abccba'' and ''deffed''.

== Reception ==
There are two published accounts of this poem one by [[Frank Raymond Leavis]]<ref name="Leavis1975">{{cite book|author=Frank Raymond Leavis|title=The living principle: "English" as a discipline of thought|date=1975|publisher=[[Chatto & Windus]]|isbn=978-1-56663-172-3|pages=120–2}}</ref> and another by [https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/english/people/ronald.carter Ronald Carter] and Walter Nash.<ref name="CarterNash1991">{{cite book|author1=Ronald Carter|author2=Walter Nash|title=Seeing Through Language: A Guide To Styles Of English Writing|date=8 January 1991|publisher=Wiley|isbn=978-0-631-15135-7|pages=123–9}}</ref>

Kennedy and Hair describes that Browning's urgent love for Elizbeth Barrett had led him to write the most sensual poem he had yet created.<ref name="KennedyHair2007"></ref>
